title: A Duality of Dust
caption: The Milky Way and zodiacal light over Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two bands of light rise side by side from the horizon above Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. One is an arm of our Milky Way, and the other, to its right, is the fainter glow of zodiacal light.

The Milky Way's glow comes from unresolved stars and other material, interrupted here and there by dark patches of dust and gas. Zodiacal light is sunlight bouncing off interplanetary dust, debris that remains from the time the Solar System formed. Because most of that dust lies in the plane the planets travel, the ecliptic, the zodiacal light traces it. Planets inside the glow confirm the line. Climbing upward from the horizon, they are Jupiter, Venus, Mars and Saturn.

The Milky Way arm appears between the DIMM1 Seeing Monitor and the decommissioned CHilean Automatic Supernova sEarch (CHASE). Other telescopes in the scene, from left to right, are the US Naval Observatory Deep South Telescope, the DIMM2 Seeing Monitor, aTmCam and the SMARTS 1.0-meter telescope.

understand.summary: A landscape photograph by Tomáš Slovinský. No camera or exposure details are published.
understand.eye: The caption gives no exposure details, but long camera exposures generally gather more light than the eye, making faint glows like zodiacal light easier to see in photographs.

explore: CTIO, a Program of NSF NOIRLab, sits in a high, dry, remote mountain setting in Chile, where sensitive equipment can pick up subtle light in the night sky. The photo was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition by Tomáš Slovinský, a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.
alt: Two parallel bands of light, the Milky Way and zodiacal light, rising above the telescopes of Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.
